summary: Describes a standard mechanism for clients to bootstrap using the iSCSI protocol. The aim is for boot clients to obtain the information needed to open a session with the iSCSI boot server. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: A computer with no disk of its own needs to find one over the network just to wake up. This memo says how it learns where to look and how to ask.

questions: what is the iscsi root path string
what are the stages of iscsi boot
how does an iscsi client find its boot server
subtitle: How a diskless computer finds an iSCSI storage server and gets enough information to boot from it.

tldr.problem: A client with no local disk may start with no IP address, no idea where its iSCSI boot server is, and not even iSCSI software.
tldr.mechanism: The client works through up to four stages: load initiator software if needed, ask DHCP or BOOTP for a Root Path string starting with "iscsi:", ask a discovery service (SLP or iSNS) to fill in gaps, then open an iSCSI session and boot.
tldr.outcome: Clients can boot from an iSCSI server across ordinary IP networks, but the RFC leaves the exact iSCSI commands to implementers and warns that iSCSI boot is a critical dependency that needs explicit administrator action to enable.

today: RFC 4173 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7146. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Booting Without a Local Disk
sections.content:
SCSI is a family of protocols for talking to I/O devices, especially storage. iSCSI carries SCSI over TCP, which suits networks that have replaced the shared bus as the system interconnect. Many diskless clients boot from remote SCSI devices, and RFC 4173 defines a standard way for them to do it with iSCSI.

The goal is narrow: let an iSCSI boot client obtain the information it needs to open an iSCSI session with the iSCSI boot server. Because that information may not all be present at power-on, the memo describes steps for collecting it.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers have no disk inside and borrow one over the network. This memo says how they find the borrowed disk.

sections.title: What a Boot Client Needs
sections.content:
The minimum a client needs to contact a boot server is its own IP address (IPv4 or IPv6), the server's iSCSI Target Name, and the mandatory iSCSI initiator capability. The default boot LUN is 0 and the default port is the well-known iSCSI port, but both can be overridden at configuration time.

The RFC lists several requirements. There must be no topology restriction beyond what is needed to establish the iSCSI session, so a client can boot from a server behind gateways or firewalls. A client may start with none of the needed information. It should be able to finish booting unattended, yet a user should have a way to enter values and skip stages. Extra software such as BOOTP or DHCP may be needed when the minimum information is not supplied.

The memo also surveys related work: RARP, TFTP, BOOTP, DHCP for IPv4 and IPv6, and the Service Location Protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: To borrow a disk, the computer needs its own address, the disk's name, and the know-how to talk to it. If it lacks any of these, it can ask helpers on the network.

sections.title: The Software and DHCP Stages
sections.content:
The boot process has stages. In the software stage, a client too small to include the iSCSI initiator can fetch initiator software from a boot server. The RFC names BOOTP and DHCP as ways of pointing to servers for software images, but explicitly recommends none of them and leaves the choice to the implementer.

In the DHCP stage, the client learns what it does not already know: its IP address, the transport endpoint of the iSCSI target (an IP address and, for TCP, a port), and the eight-byte LUN. If the client already has everything, it can go straight to the Boot stage. An address can come from BOOTP, DHCP (v4 or v6) or IPv6 autoconfiguration. DHCP settings may forbid distributing iSCSI boot information, in which case this stage cannot be used.
sections.plainLanguage: First the computer may fetch a small helper program. Then it asks the network helper for its own address and for directions to the disk.

sections.title: The Root Path String
sections.content:
A BOOTP or DHCP server MAY tell a client how to reach its boot device using the variable-length Root Path option. For iSCSI boot, the option's use is reserved by starting the string with iscsi:. The value is a UTF-8 string:

"iscsi:"<servername>":"<protocol>":"<port>":"<LUN>":"<targetname>

Only targetname is required; the others are optional and left blank when there is no value. Root Path is not currently defined for DHCPv6, but if it is defined later, the iSCSI use applies.

  • servername: a domain name, literal IPv4 address or literal IPv6 address, following the URI specification. Name compression MUST NOT be used.
  • protocol: decimal transport number, default 6 (TCP), which is the only approved transport.
  • port: decimal port, defaulting to the well-known iSCSI port.
  • LUN: hexadecimal, default LUN 0 when blank. When present it MUST be four groups of four hex digits separated by hyphens, such as 4752-3A4F-6b7e-2F99. Up to three leading zeros per group may be dropped, and trailing all-zero groups may be omitted, so 4186-9 means 4186-0009-0000-0000.
  • targetname: the iSCSI Name that uniquely identifies the target.

If servername is given, the client uses it to reach the server in the Boot stage. If not, the target name is used in the Discovery Service stage.
sections.plainLanguage: The network helper hands over one line of text, like an address label with parts separated by colons. Only the disk's name is a must; the rest have sensible defaults.

sections.title: The Discovery Service Stage
sections.content:
This stage is needed when the BOOTP or DHCP server knows of no iSCSI boot servers, or cannot supply the minimum information other than the target name. The discovery service may be based on SLP or on iSNS.

With a target name from the DHCP stage, the client asks SLP (query string 1 of the iSCSI Target Concrete Service Type Template) or iSNS (a Device Attribute Query) to resolve it to an IP address and port. If the port conflicts with the one from DHCP, the implementer may try both.

With no target name, the client can query SLP with query string 4 to get a list of boot servers it may access, or ask iSNS whether the targets in a particular Discovery Domain are bootable. If the list is empty, what happens next is up to the implementer. Otherwise the client may contact any server in the list, in any order.
sections.plainLanguage: If the helper only knows the disk's name, the computer asks a directory where that name lives. If it does not even know a name, it asks the directory for a list of disks it may use.

sections.title: The Boot Stage
sections.content: Once the client has the minimum information, it opens an iSCSI session and boots. The RFC deliberately does not specify the sequence of iSCSI commands, because vendors and equipment differ too much to agree on a common subset. The session established for boot may be taken over by the booted software.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the computer knows where the disk is, it connects and starts up. How exactly it does that is left to each maker.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Verifying the boot image itself is out of scope. Unlike BOOTP image loading, the identity of an image may not be known when the Boot stage starts, and images may load further images, so each image-loading program should verify what it loads in its own way.

Enabling iSCSI boot creates a critical dependence on an external system, so it SHOULD NOT be enabled or put high in the boot order without explicit administrative action. A client must make sure a server is authorized to send it information, for example from a pre-configured list of servers.

The software stage SHOULD NOT be part of a secure iSCSI boot, so the needed software is assumed to be resident on the client. Where DHCP is used, the client SHOULD implement DHCP authentication, and the reply SHOULD include the server name as an IP address to avoid relying on DNS or a discovery service. SLP and iSNS clients SHOULD support IPsec. For the final session, IPsec and in-band authentication SHOULD be implemented per the iSCSI guidelines; clients are expected to support only pre-shared key authentication in IKE, and IKE main mode SHOULD NOT be used when the host address is assigned dynamically. A boot image that inherits an iSCSI session also inherits its security properties.
sections.plainLanguage: Booting from the network means trusting the network, so the computer should check that whoever answers is allowed to. And the owner should turn this feature on on purpose.

items.title: servername
items.text: Optional. Domain name or literal IPv4 or IPv6 address.

items.title: port
items.text: Optional. Defaults to the well-known iSCSI port.

items.title: LUN
items.text: Optional. Four groups of hex digits; blank means LUN 0.

items.title: targetname
items.text: Required. The iSCSI Name of the target.
